title: Transit statement
topic: A friend reasons backward from a $3.50 transit charge under an exclusive fare rule
blurb: A friend is checking a charge on a shared transit account.
prompt: A friend just sent this in the group chat. Tap a line if something doesn't add up, or let it pass.

segments.label: The fare rule
segments.text: Our metro card only charges the $3.50 peak fare when you tap in between 7 and 9 AM; every other tap-in is $2.25, and this card has no passes or surcharges.

segments.label: The receipt
segments.text: My cousin swears he slept past 9:30 yesterday, yet his statement shows a single $3.50 ride deduction for the whole day.

segments.label: The call
segments.text: If the statement charged $3.50, then his card was definitely tapped in between 7 and 9 AM.

segments.label: The hunch
segments.text: Either he's mixing up which day he slept in, or somebody else borrowed his card.

conclusion: Because $3.50 only occurs on a 7–9 AM tap-in, seeing a $3.50 charge proves the card tapped in between 7 and 9 AM.

diagnosis: Transit systems usually charge peak fare during evening rush hour too, so 7–9 AM can't be the only window.
Two $2.25 rides don't add up to $3.50, but a transfer fee could still push an off-peak ride to $3.50.
Saying 'every other tap-in is $2.25' leaves out tap-out adjustments when you ride across fare zones.
Stating a rule in the forward direction ('7–9 AM gives $3.50') never lets you reverse it later.
fix: Check whether evening rush hour (5–7 PM) also charges $3.50 before ruling it out.
Verify whether cross-zone surcharges apply to this line.
Note that a partial pass credit could still produce a $3.50 charge off-peak.
Check the station timestamp instead of relying on the fare schedule.

diagnosis: Transit statements often post charges a day late, so yesterday's $3.50 is almost certainly from the day before.
A single $3.50 deduction could be a missed tap-out penalty from a $2.25 ride after 9:30.
He could have tapped in at 9:35 and still been charged $3.50 if the gate clock was slow.
One $3.50 line item could be two smaller charges bundled together at midnight.
fix: Check the posting date vs the ride date on the card statement.
Ask whether he forgot to tap out on his afternoon trip.
Look up the turnstile entry time rather than trusting the dollar amount.
Check if $3.50 is a daily cap combining a bus and a train.

diagnosis: You're flipping an 'if A then B' rule backward into 'if B then A' — a $3.50 charge doesn't prove a 7–9 AM tap-in.
Just because 7–9 AM costs $3.50 doesn't rule out other ways to hit $3.50 later in the day.
Reasoning from the price back to the clock time is invalid unless you also see the gate's timestamp.
Even if 7–9 AM guarantees $3.50, seeing $3.50 only makes 7–9 AM *likely*, not definite.
fix: Say a $3.50 charge makes a 7–9 AM tap-in plausible, not definite.
Don't reverse the fare rule — check the actual entry timestamp on the app.
Rule out other $3.50 triggers first before blaming the 7–9 AM window.
Remember that 'if 7–9 AM then $3.50' never implies 'if $3.50 then 7–9 AM'.

diagnosis: False dilemma: there's a third option — he rode after 9:30 and got billed $3.50 for some other reason.
Even if someone else used the card, that wouldn't explain why the cousin forgot lending it out.
Jumping to 'someone borrowed his card' ignores that the $3.50 could have been an evening peak ride.
He might have tapped in right at 9:00 AM sharp, which still matches sleeping until almost 9.
fix: Add a third possibility: an off-peak ride triggered a $3.50 charge for another reason.
Ask him if he took an evening train instead of accusing him of mixing up days.
Check whether he woke up at 8:55 rather than 9:30 before blaming another person.
Wait for the app's ride history before narrowing it down to two explanations.

clean_segments: Our metro card only charges the $3.50 peak fare when you tap in between 7 and 9 AM; every other tap-in is $2.25, and this card has no passes or surcharges.
My cousin swears he slept past 9:30 yesterday, yet his statement shows a single $3.50 ride deduction for the whole day.
If the statement charged $3.50, then his card was definitely tapped in between 7 and 9 AM.
Either he's mixing up which day he slept in, or somebody else borrowed his card.
clean_conclusion: Usually flipping an 'if' rule backward is a trap — except line 1 already locked it down to 'only between 7 and 9 AM, every other tap-in is $2.25, no surcharges.' With no other way to get $3.50, working backward actually holds.
